headline: The West Cut Narrowed Since the Spring Blow — Bass Are Riding the New Funnel
subhead: A tighter throat at Moriches Inlet is concentrating bait and bass on the ebb, while jumbo bluefish work the boils off Cupsogue and fluke settle onto the flats.
body_markdown:
I walked the west jetty at Cupsogue on Tuesday's low and the sand tells a story if you know how to read it. The bar that sat off the tip back in May has migrated maybe fifteen, twenty yards closer to the rocks, and the main channel through the throat has pinched down noticeably — I'd guess it's running two, three feet shallower on the edges than it was in April. That's what a summer's worth of southerly wind swell does to this inlet. It's not a storm cut, it's a slow squeeze, sand walking in off the ocean side and stacking against the jetty face. The upshot: the current through that narrower throat is running harder than it has all season, and hard current through a tight gap means one thing on the ebb — everything gets funneled, bait and predators both, into a smaller lane than it used to be.

That's exactly what's showing up in the bass fishing. Guys working the last two hours of the outgoing off the north side of the inlet, right where the flat drops from four feet down into that 15 to 18-foot channel edge, are finding stripers stacked on the lip of that drop. Bucktails in the half-ounce to three-quarter range, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and let sink to the bottom before a slow hop back — that's putting fish in the boat, mostly slot-class fish in the 28 to 34-inch range with a scattering of shorts mixed in. After dark, the eel bite off the rocks has been the more consistent play — snake a 10 to 12-inch live eel along the current seam where the fast water meets the eddy behind the jetty rocks, let it swim naturally, and you're in business. This lines up with what's been happening farther east — heavy fish staging tight on current edges and visible boils rather than roaming open water. Moriches is doing its own version of that pattern, just on a smaller stage.

Bluefish are the wild card right now and they're not subtle about it. There's been a push of larger blues, some pushing double digits, working bunker schools that get pinned against the inlet's outer bar on the last of the ebb. If you see the water nervous and diving terns working a patch off Cupsogue, that's your window — metal, Deadly Dicks or Hopkins, worked fast through the melee. Just don't expect it to hold; these blitzes have been short and mobile, here for twenty minutes and gone. I've had two good windows this week and missed three others because I was five minutes late getting the boat turned around.

Fluke have quietly become the better bet if you want a full box rather than a highlight reel. The flats inside the inlet — from the Pattersquash side down through the deeper guts off Tuthill Point — are holding decent numbers of keeper fluke in eight to twelve feet of water. Drifting bucktails tipped with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets, or a simple high-low rig with squid strips and spearing, has been the ticket on the moving tide, either direction, though the last two hours of the incoming has been putting bigger fish over the rail as bait gets pushed up onto the flats. This tracks with what's been reported up and down the South Shore and East End all month — the fluke run has genuinely improved since June, and Moriches is holding up its end. Nothing over 6 pounds that I've heard of locally, but a steady grade of 18 to 22-inch fish keeps a cooler interesting.

Weakfish are around but thin — I'm hearing occasional fish taken incidentally on soft plastics worked slow along the bay-side grass edges near Westhampton, nothing you'd plan a trip around. Porgies are filling the gap for bottom guys — the deeper holes off Smith Point and inside the bay proper are holding good numbers on sandworm and clam, standard high-low rigs, nothing fancy needed. Blackfish season's closed through the summer, so that's a fall conversation.

Water on the ocean side has stayed choppy and short-period all week — that 3 to 4-foot windswell at a quick four-second interval isn't a groundswell, it's local wind chop, and it's been enough to keep the surf grubby and limit bar access at Cupsogue to the early morning calm windows. Inside the bay, temperatures are comfortably into summer range, warm enough that the bass bite is concentrating around structure and current rather than open flats during the heat of the day. That thermal split between a churned-up ocean front and a stable, warm interior is exactly why the inlet throat has become the productive zone — it's the seam between the two systems, and seams are where fish set up shop.

Looking ahead, if the wind backs off out of the south for a stretch, I'd put my money on the dawn outgoing at the inlet for bass and blues both, working that narrowed channel edge I mentioned. If it stays blown out, shift effort inside — the fluke flats don't care much what the ocean's doing, and that's been the more dependable program the last two weeks anyway. I'd carry both game plans this weekend and let the first hour on the water decide which one you fish.
